questions.stem: If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², what is f(g(x))?
questions.explanation: f(g(x)) applies g first, then f: f(x²) = 2x² + 1. The expression (2x + 1)² is g(f(x)), the composition in the other order.

questions.stem: If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², what is g(f(3))?
questions.explanation: f(3) = 7, then g(7) = 49. Applying g first gives f(g(3)) = f(9) = 19, which is the other composition.

questions.stem: For functions f and g, when is the composite function f ∘ g, given by f(g(x)), defined?
options: when the range of f is a subset of the domain of g
when the range of g is the same as the range of f
when the range of g is a subset of the domain of f
when the domain of g is a subset of the domain of f
questions.explanation: Every output of g must be an allowed input of f. The condition with the range of f inside the domain of g is the one for g ∘ f.

questions.stem: f(x) = √x for x ≥ 0 and g(x) = x − 4 for all real x. What is the largest domain on which f(g(x)) is defined?
questions.explanation: f(g(x)) = √(x − 4) needs x − 4 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 4. Using the domain of f, x ≥ 0, ignores that g changes the input first.

questions.stem: f(x) = 1/x for x ≠ 0 and g(x) = x² − 9 for all real x. What is the largest domain of f(g(x))?
questions.explanation: f(g(x)) = 1/(x² − 9) needs g(x) ≠ 0, so x ≠ ±3. Excluding only x = 0 applies the domain of f to x instead of to g(x).

questions.stem: f(x) = √x for x ≥ 0 and g(x) = 4 − x². On the largest domain where f(g(x)) is defined, what is its range?
questions.explanation: f(g(x)) = √(4 − x²) is defined for −2 ≤ x ≤ 2, where 4 − x² takes the values 0 to 4. Its square root then runs from 0 to 2.

questions.stem: f(x) = x² for all real x and g(x) = √(x − 1) for x ≥ 1. What is the largest domain of g(f(x))?
questions.explanation: g(f(x)) = √(x² − 1) needs x² ≥ 1, which holds for x ≤ −1 as well as x ≥ 1. Taking only x ≥ 1 copies the domain of g and misses the negative values.

questions.stem: h(x) = (3x − 1)⁵ is written as f(g(x)). Which pair of functions works?
questions.explanation: The inner function g(x) = 3x − 1 is applied first and then raised to the power 5. Swapping them gives 3x⁵ − 1, and the other pairs give (3x)⁵ − 1 and (3x − 3)⁵.

questions.stem: f(x) = x + 2 and g(x) = x². For which x is f(g(x)) = g(f(x))?
questions.explanation: f(g(x)) = x² + 2 and g(f(x)) = (x + 2)² = x² + 4x + 4. Equating gives 4x + 4 = 2, so x = −1/2.

questions.stem: Which test shows from its graph that a function is one-to-one?
options: every horizontal line meets the graph at most once
every vertical line meets the graph at most once
every horizontal line meets the graph at least once
every vertical line meets the graph exactly once
questions.explanation: One-to-one means no two x values give the same y value, so no horizontal line can cross twice. The vertical line test only checks that the graph is a function.

questions.stem: Which function is one-to-one over all real numbers?
questions.explanation: x³ + 1 is strictly increasing, so each y value comes from one x. The others repeat values, for example (−1)² − 1 = 1² − 1 and |−2| = |2|.

questions.stem: f(x) = x² + 6x + 5 is one-to-one on the domain x ≥ a. What is the smallest possible value of a?
questions.explanation: f(x) = (x + 3)² − 4 has its turning point at x = −3, and it is increasing for x ≥ −3. The zeros, −5 and −1, are not where the graph turns.

questions.stem: On which of these domains is f(x) = x² − 4x one-to-one?
questions.explanation: f(x) = (x − 2)² − 4 turns at x = 2. Any domain containing values on both sides of 2, such as [1, ∞), includes pairs like x = 1 and x = 3 with the same output.

questions.stem: The function f is given by f(x) = 3x − 6 for all real x. What is its inverse function?
questions.explanation: Swap x and y: x = 3y − 6, so y = (x + 6)/3. The reciprocal 1/(3x − 6) is not the inverse function; f⁻¹ does not mean 1/f.

questions.stem: How are the domain and range of f⁻¹ related to those of a one-to-one function f?
options: the domain of f⁻¹ is the domain of f, and its range is the reciprocal of each value
the domain of f⁻¹ is all real numbers whatever f is
the domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f
they are the same as the domain and range of f
questions.explanation: An inverse swaps inputs and outputs, so the domain and range swap. This is why the domain of an inverse often needs care, as with square roots.

questions.stem: f(x) = √(x − 1) for x ≥ 1. What is f⁻¹(x), with its domain?
questions.explanation: Swapping gives x = √(y − 1), so y = x² + 1. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, which is x ≥ 0, so the inverse is only the right half of the parabola.

questions.stem: f(x) = (x + 2)/(x − 1) for x ≠ 1. What is f⁻¹(x)?
questions.explanation: From x = (y + 2)/(y − 1): xy − x = y + 2, so y(x − 1) = x + 2 and y = (x + 2)/(x − 1). The function is its own inverse, so its graph is symmetric about y = x.

questions.stem: f(x) = 2/(x − 3) + 1 for x ≠ 3. What is f⁻¹(x)?
questions.explanation: From x = 2/(y − 3) + 1: x − 1 = 2/(y − 3), so y − 3 = 2/(x − 1) and y = 2/(x − 1) + 3. The asymptotes x = 3, y = 1 become x = 1, y = 3.

questions.stem: f(x) = x² − 2x for x ≤ 1. What is f⁻¹(x), with its domain?
questions.explanation: f(x) = (x − 1)² − 1, so swapping gives (y − 1)² = x + 1 and y = 1 ± √(x + 1). The range of f⁻¹ must be y ≤ 1, the domain of f, so take the negative root.

questions.stem: The point (2, 7) lies on the graph of a one-to-one function f. Which point must lie on the graph of f⁻¹?
questions.explanation: The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x, which swaps the coordinates. The point (2, 1/7) would be on y = 1/f(x), not on the inverse.

questions.stem: f(x) = (x² + 6)/5 for x ≥ 0 is increasing. Where do the graphs of y = f(x) and y = f⁻¹(x) meet?
questions.explanation: For an increasing function the graphs meet on y = x, so solve (x² + 6)/5 = x: x² − 5x + 6 = 0, giving x = 2 or 3. Negative values lie outside the domain x ≥ 0.

questions.stem: f(x) = x³ − 1. What is f⁻¹(7)?
questions.explanation: f⁻¹(7) is the x with f(x) = 7: x³ − 1 = 7, so x³ = 8 and x = 2. The value 342 is f(7), and 1/342 is 1/f(7).

questions.stem: Which is the definition of the absolute value |x| of a real number x?
options: −x when x ≥ 0, and x when x < 0
x² when x ≥ 0, and −x² when x < 0
x when x ≥ 0, and −x when x < 0
x when x ≥ 0, and x when x < 0
questions.explanation: For negative x, −x is positive, so |x| is never negative; for example |−5| = −(−5) = 5. It also measures the distance from x to 0 on the number line.
|−7| = 7 and |3 − 5| = |−2| = 2, so the result is 7 − 2 = 5. Working out the brackets as −7 − 2 forgets that each absolute value is positive.

questions.stem: What are the solutions of |2x − 3| = 7?
questions.explanation: 2x − 3 = 7 gives x = 5, and 2x − 3 = −7 gives x = −2. Both satisfy the equation, so ignoring the negative case loses a solution.

questions.stem: What is the solution of |x − 1| < 3?
questions.explanation: The distance from x to 1 is less than 3, so −3 < x − 1 < 3 and −2 < x < 4. The values x < −2 or x > 4 solve |x − 1| > 3 instead.

questions.stem: The graph of y = |x − 2| + 1 is a V shape. Where is its vertex?
questions.explanation: The graph of y = |x| is moved 2 units right and 1 unit up, so its vertex moves from (0, 0) to (2, 1). Shifting left instead gives (−2, 1).

questions.stem: What are the solutions of |x + 1| = 2x − 4?
questions.explanation: x + 1 = 2x − 4 gives x = 5, which checks: 6 = 6. −(x + 1) = 2x − 4 gives x = 1, but then the right side is −2, which an absolute value cannot equal, so x = 1 is rejected.

questions.stem: Starting from the graph of y = f(x), which change produces the graph of y = |f(x)|?
options: reflect the whole graph in the x-axis
reflect the parts below the x-axis in the x-axis
reflect the parts left of the y-axis in the y-axis
replace the part left of the y-axis with a reflection of the right part
questions.explanation: Negative y values become positive and the rest is unchanged, so only the parts below the x-axis flip up. Replacing the left half by a mirror of the right half gives y = f(|x|).

questions.stem: Where does the graph of y = |x² − 4| have a local maximum?
questions.explanation: The minimum (0, −4) of y = x² − 4 is below the x-axis, so it reflects to a local maximum at (0, 4). The points (±2, 0) become sharp minimum points.

questions.stem: How many real solutions does |x² − 4| = 4 have?
questions.explanation: Either x² − 4 = 4, giving x = ±2√2, or x² − 4 = −4, giving x = 0 only. The line y = 4 touches the local maximum at (0, 4), so there are three solutions.

questions.stem: About which line is the graph of y = f(|x|) always symmetric?
questions.explanation: f(|−x|) = f(|x|), so y = f(|x|) is an even function. Its graph keeps the part of y = f(x) for x ≥ 0 and mirrors it in the y-axis.

questions.stem: What are the x-intercepts of y = (|x| − 2)²?
questions.explanation: This is y = f(|x|) for f(x) = (x − 2)², which touches the x-axis at x = 2. Mirroring the right half in the y-axis adds x = −2.

questions.stem: f(x) = x² − 2x − 3. What are the x-intercepts of y = f(|x|)?
questions.explanation: f(x) = (x − 3)(x + 1), so for x ≥ 0 the only zero is x = 3. The left half is the mirror image of the right half, giving x = −3; the zero at x = −1 is discarded with the old left half.

questions.stem: Each zero of f(x) corresponds to which feature of the graph of y = 1/f(x)?
questions.explanation: Where f(x) = 0, 1/f(x) is undefined and grows without bound nearby, giving vertical asymptotes. 1/f(x) can never be zero, so it has no x-intercepts.

questions.stem: f(x) = x² − 2x + 5 has a minimum at (1, 4). What does y = 1/f(x) have at x = 1?
questions.explanation: Where a positive f is smallest, 1/f is largest, so the minimum becomes a maximum with value 1/4. There is no asymptote, since f(x) = (x − 1)² + 4 is never 0.

questions.stem: f(x) = 2x − 6. What are the asymptotes of y = 1/f(x)?
questions.explanation: The zero of f at x = 3 gives a vertical asymptote, and as |x| grows |f(x)| grows without bound, so 1/f(x) → 0. The horizontal asymptote is y = 0.

questions.stem: On an interval where f(x) is positive and increasing, how does y = 1/f(x) behave?
questions.explanation: 1/f has the same sign as f, so it is positive. As f increases, its reciprocal gets smaller, so 1/f is decreasing.

questions.stem: At which x values do the graphs of y = x² − 3 and y = 1/(x² − 3) meet?
questions.explanation: y = f(x) and y = 1/f(x) meet where f(x) = 1/f(x), that is f(x) = ±1. Then x² = 4 or x² = 2. At x = ±√3, f is 0 and the reciprocal has asymptotes.
